label: Quadrilateral Sets and Liftings
notes: Welcome to chapter eight, printed pages 129 through 144. We study the six points a complete quadrilateral cuts on a transversal line and the bracket condition that ties them together. Then we lift planar figures into space so incidence theorems like Desargues become almost obvious from a three dimensional shadow.

label: The Complete Quadrilateral
notes: A complete quadrilateral is four lines in general position together with their six pairwise intersection points. Stress the count: four lines, six vertices, and three diagonals joining opposite vertices. This is the dual companion of the complete quadrangle, four points and their six joining lines, and both will feed the same six point invariant.

label: Six Points on a Transversal
notes: Cut the figure with any line that misses the vertices. Each of the four lines meets it once and each of the two diagonals meets it once, giving six marked points. Grouped into three opposite pairs these six points are the quadrilateral set. The key claim is that they are not arbitrary; one algebraic relation always binds them.

label: The Bracket Condition
notes: Here is the defining equation. Using two by two brackets of homogeneous line coordinates, opposite pairs a-d, b-e, c-f satisfy the product of three brackets on the left equal to the product on the right. Point out that this is a projective statement, invariant under any projective map of the line, so it survives every change of transversal.

label: Affine Slope Form
notes: Choosing an affine chart turns brackets into coordinate differences, so the condition reads as a product of three factors equal to another. The notebook builds the six points from slopes of the lines through four finite points, which guarantees the relation. This is the form we actually compute with and perturb in the lab.

label: Generalizing the Harmonic Relation
notes: When two of the three pairs coincide the quadrilateral set degenerates to the classical harmonic relation with cross ratio minus one. So a quadrilateral set is the natural six point cousin of a four point harmonic quadruple. Emphasize that the same incidence machinery, the complete quadrangle, produces both, which is why von Staudt arithmetic reappears here.

label: Five Points Force the Sixth
notes: Because the condition is a single equation, fixing five of the six coordinates determines the last one whenever the denominator is nonzero. This is the recognition test: given six points on a line, they come from a planar quadrilateral exactly when the bracket balance holds. Degeneracies are precisely vanishing denominators or collisions, nothing mysterious.

label: Liftings: Shadows from Higher Space
notes: A lifting realizes a flat incidence figure as the projection, the shadow, of points and lines living in higher dimensional space. Collinear points on the line are raised to heights so that the requested triples become genuinely collinear up in the plane or space. The lifting exists exactly when a rank condition holds, the same bracket balance in disguise.

label: The Lifting Matrix
notes: Encode each required collinear triple as a linear equation on the unknown heights. Stack them into a matrix. A nontrivial, non-affine lift exists when this matrix drops rank, leaving a null vector that is not simply a constant or linear height. Rank three with a genuine null direction is the computational signature the notebook checks.

label: Desargues in Three Dimensions
notes: Two triangles perspective from a point are the shadow of two triangles lying in two distinct planes of space. Those planes meet in a line, and the three pairs of corresponding sides meet on that line of intersection. Projecting down, that line becomes the Desargues axis. In space the theorem is just two planes sharing a line.

label: Why the 3D View Makes It Obvious
notes: The space picture removes all casework. Corresponding sides lie in a common plane through the center, so each pair must meet, and every such meeting lies in both triangle planes, hence on their shared line. Collapsing the third dimension projects a true spatial incidence to a planar theorem. Liftings turn hard plane proofs into easy space observations.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Recap the through line: one bracket balance underlies the quadrilateral set, the harmonic special case, von Staudt arithmetic, the five forces six reconstruction, and the rank test for liftings. Liftings then explain incidence theorems as shadows. Leave students with the habit of asking what higher figure casts this plane configuration as its shadow.
